body_html:
Gas is $4.29. Consumer sentiment is the second-lowest reading since 1978. And a sit-down restaurant chain just reported mid-single-digit traffic growth on top of three years of double-digit comps.

With a toddler and a 1-month old at home, I admit we haven’t gone out as much as before. But whenever we do, I feel the restaurant inflation plus the expected 25% tip! And yet each time we go out, the restaurants are full. If we don’t reserve ahead of time, we end up waiting for hours!

The numbers say the same thing. Regular unleaded is $4.29 a gallon, 40% above a year earlier, and 56% of Americans told the University of Michigan that prices were hurting their finances. Five days later, a casual-dining operator reported 6% more guests through its doors than a year earlier. Same-store sales grew double digits for the third year in a row. Restaurant margins went up.

You’d expect Mr. Market to pay up for that. He hasn’t. The shares sit 20% below their August high, the one factor its quant score flags as weak is Valuation, and most of what’s written about the name argues one of two things: the comps are about to lap themselves into the ground, or the multiple is too rich for a sit-down restaurant.

I think both arguments look at the wrong part of the business. The comps are the result of the last three years. The next three years run on something Mr. Market isn’t pricing at all: a store base running 1,000 guests a week below its own historical peak, a new-unit program that earns 18-20% cash on cash, and a buyback that retires 3-5% of the shares every year. I rebuilt the model around that plan and the bear case clears the hurdle I ask for.

I picked this name in 2024. It is up 330% since then and I still see upside in the stock. Below is the full deep dive, the rebuilt model, 10,000 Monte Carlo runs, and the rating change.

Table of Contents

  • TLDR

  • How the stock ranks

  • The P&L of one restaurant, in plain English

  • The industry: a $116B pie and who is eating it

  • Supply chain: beef, chicken and 85k people

  • How a tired brand got 1,000 more guests a week

  • The flywheel in numbers

  • The next chapter: three levers Mr. Market isn’t pricing

  • Management and capital allocation

  • The smaller brand that drags

  • Valuation

  • Steel-manning the bear

  • The Monte Carlo: 10,000 runs

  • From HOLD to BUY

  • Verdict

TLDR

  • The company is Brinker International [], the owner of Chili’s Grill & Bar and Maggiano’s Little Italy. Chili’s is 92% of revenue and 94% of adjusted profit, so this is a Chili’s investment (not Chile, for those check out my section here :) ).

  • Chili’s has grown same-store sales for 22 straight quarters and beaten the casual-dining industry on traffic for 12 straight. Q1 FY2027 comps were +10.1% on +6.4% traffic, lapping +21% and +14% in the two prior years. Restaurant operating margin reached 17.7%, +150bps y/y.

  • The turnaround phase is over. The next three years run on three levers the bear case ignores: throughput headroom of 1,000 guests per restaurant per week vs. the historical peak, 30 new units a year by FY2029 at 18-20% cash-on-cash returns, and a buyback of 3-5% of the shares every year.

  • Key risk: Chili’s carries the whole company, and a consumer under $4.29 gas is already managing the check on alcohol and dessert. If traffic goes negative, the margin leverage that built this story runs in reverse.

  • I bought EAT at $51 and it is already +330% up. I had EAT as a HOLD for most of the past 12 months. I’m moving EAT from HOLD to BUY. Fair value $247 (+19%). Bear $188 (-9%), bull $298 (+44%), risk-reward 2.1 to 1. The Monte Carlo clears today’s price in 89% of 10,000 runs.

How EAT ranks

RankedStocks.com scores EAT at 77, Strong, in the 85th percentile of its global peers. Four of the five factors sit in the Strong or Elite band. The fifth is the whole debate.

Valuation 20. P/E at 19.5x trailing and 19.7x forward, EV/EBITDA at 12.5x, and EV to invested capital at 5.1x all score in the bottom half of the 588 US consumer discretionary names in the peer set. Price to book at 22.3x scores 3, which tells you more about $444M of buybacks on a $444M equity base than about the price of the business. The forward multiples are the part I’d argue with: 19.7x forward earnings for a company guiding to double-digit EPS growth with a 3-5% annual share-count shrink is the market’s view of a restaurant stock rather than of this restaurant.

Growth 67. Trailing revenue growth of 7.9% and EPS growth of 30.8% score in the 60s. The forward column is what holds the factor down: consensus forward EBITDA growth of 8.8% scores 44 and forward ROE growth scores 24. Mr. Market expects the growth rate to halve. The model below argues it holds in the 6-7% range for three more years because unit growth and reimages start adding on top of comps.

Profitability 77. ROE of 123%, return on total assets of 17.3% and ROIC of 25.5% all score in the high 80s and 90s. The one sub-score in the single digits is gross margin at 4.9%, and that is a data-vendor definition which loads restaurant labour and occupancy into cost of revenue. Read EBIT margin at 10.7% and net margin at 8.4% instead; both sit in the top third.

Sentiment 86 and Outlook 67. EPS has beaten consensus in 84% of the last 136 reports, and the latest print beat by 13%. The sentiment score is the share price run of the last year showing up as a factor, and it is the score that would fall fastest if the comps disappoint.

Against the nine restaurant peers RankedStocks lists, EAT has the second-highest forward revenue CAGR at 5.4% behind Aramark [], a forward EBIT margin of 10.6% that only the four UK pub groups beat, and the second-lowest Valuation score. One of the fastest-growing, most profitable names in the table is priced like it isn’t.

RankedStocks.com is free. You can run the same factor work, the DCF, the reverse DCF and the Monte Carlo on any ticker yourself.

The P&L of one restaurant, in plain English

Forget the holding company for a minute and look at a single Chili’s.

It is a box with a bar, a kitchen and a dining room, open from lunch through late night. In FY2026 the average company-owned Chili’s served 4,200 guests a week and took in $5.0M of sales for the year, which works out to $23 per guest including drinks. Alcohol is 9% of that. The guest who orders the $10.99 “3 for Me” (a drink, an appetizer and an entrée) is the floor of the check; the table that adds a margarita and a Triple Dipper is the ceiling.

Out of every $100 of sales, $25.90 goes to food and drink, $31.50 to the people cooking and serving it, and $24.80 to the building: rent, utilities, repairs, advertising, insurance and delivery fees. What is left, $17.80, is restaurant operating margin. Chili’s on its own runs at 18.5%; Maggiano’s runs at 10.1%.

Those four lines are the whole thesis in miniature, because two of them are fixed and two are not. Food cost moves with commodities and with what people order. Labour and occupancy are fixed per shift and per lease. So every extra guest who walks in on a Tuesday night is served by the same cooks under the same roof, and most of what that guest spends falls through to margin. That is why a 9.2% comp in FY2026 turned into 30bps of margin improvement and why a 10.1% comp in Q1 FY2027 turned into 150bps. The reverse is also true, which is the bear case.

A new Chili’s costs $5-6M to build and is expected to open at $5M of sales and 18% margin. That is $900K of restaurant profit on a $5.5M build, or 18-20% cash on cash before corporate overhead. A business that can reinvest at 18-20% when its cost of capital is 8% should be building restaurants, and for the first time in a decade it is.

The industry: a $116B pie and who is eating it

American casual dining is the sit-down tier between fast food and the white tablecloth: a server, a bar, a $20-30 check, a 45-minute visit. Circana sizes it at $116B a year across chains and independents. The National Restaurant Association expects the whole restaurant industry to reach $1.55 trillion in 2026 with real growth of 1.3%, and 60% of operators told it traffic was softer last year than the year before. Three currents move this pie, and all three favour the biggest operators.

The first is price. The menu at a full-service restaurant rose 3.8% in the year to September 2026 while groceries rose 1.8%. The gap between eating out and eating in has been widening for four years, and the household that notices it either cooks or trades down. Trading down used to mean fast food. Chili’s built “3 for Me” to take that trade: a drink, an appetizer and an entrée at a table for $10.99, with a chicken sandwich management says is 80% bigger than the leading fast-food version. The chain that can sell a full sit-down meal for the price of a drive-through combo has a structural traffic advantage in the environment we are in.

The second is consolidation. Casual dining is consolidating around its strongest brands. In the Technomic Top 500, Chili’s grew US system sales 20.6% in 2025 to $5.5B and passed Olive Garden to become the second-largest casual-dining chain in the country behind Texas Roadhouse. Applebee’s shrank 0.8% and closed 29 units. Within the $116B, Chili’s holds a 5% share.

The third is the consumer. The Michigan sentiment index hit a record low of 44.8 in May 2026 when the Iran conflict pushed gas toward $5 in parts of the country, and the October reading was the second-lowest on record. When trips get cut, the cut lands on the restaurants a family trusts least. Black Box Intelligence, the industry’s traffic benchmark, had casual-dining traffic down 2% over the three years to FY2026. Chili’s traffic was up 20% over the same window.

Supply chain: beef, chicken and 85k people

What does a Chili’s buy, and from whom? Three things dominate: protein, labour and leases.

On protein, EAT negotiates with the major suppliers itself and uses purchase agreements to lock the volatile items, with everything delivered through pre-qualified distributors. The 10-K doesn’t name the vendors. The commodity that matters most is beef, because burgers are a $600M category and the “Big Smasher” and “Big QP” are two of the three value heroes. Beef is the wrong place to be exposed right now: the US cattle herd fell to 86.2M head in January 2026, the smallest since 1951, ground beef hit a record $6.69 a pound, and the industry sees no serious rebuilding, which means two more years of elevated prices. EAT’s commodity basket ran 4.4% inflation in Q4 FY2026 and 3.3% in Q1 FY2027, meat and seafood doing most of the damage, and the CFO modelled 4%, 3%, 2% and 1% through the four quarters of FY2027. The third hero, the $10.99 “Big Crispy” chicken sandwich, is chicken, the cheaper protein, which is not a coincidence.

On labour, EAT employed 85k people, 82% of them part-time hourly. Wage inflation ran 2.6% in Q1 and the CFO guides 3% for the year. The number that changed the economics is turnover: hourly turnover fell from 145% in FY2023 to 84% in FY2026 and manager turnover from 24% to 20%. A kitchen that keeps its cooks serves faster and wastes less, and 87% of new general managers were promoted from inside. Almost 80% of GMs now earn above $100K. That is a cost line, and it is also the moat.

On leases, EAT rents most of its boxes. Operating lease liabilities stood at $1.19B long-term at year end against $445M of actual debt, and that distinction matters when you read any leverage figure on this name. Lease-adjusted leverage is 1.4x, down from 3.7x three years ago, and the target is below 2.0x.

Who does it sell to? Everyone, which is the point. Chili’s served 239M guests in FY2026, up 40M in two years, and the growth came from Gen Z and millennials without losing the Gen X and boomer core. Marketing targets millennial families and Gen Z through streaming and social video rather than linear TV. The viral “Triple Dipper” moment in April 2024 was the spark; the deck’s point, and I think the right one, is that a viral moment only compounds if the food and the service hold up when the new guest shows up, and the frequency chart says it did.

How a tired brand got 1,000 more guests a week

Chili’s is 51 years old. In FY2023 it was a tired brand with a bloated menu, 145% hourly turnover, a $3.3M average unit volume and an 11.2% restaurant margin, and the parent had $907M of net debt. Kevin Hochman came in as the CEO in 2022 from KFC, where he had run the US business, and the turnaround he ran is the one the rest of the category is now studying.

The playbook had four parts, and the order matters.

First, make the restaurant easier to run. Chili’s cut the menu by 29% of items, removed tasks that didn’t touch the guest, shut the virtual brands and ghost kitchens, and spent $180M of incremental labour putting more people in the critical positions. Managers got a one-page shift checklist instead of eight pages. The point of all of it was throughput: a kitchen that can handle more guests without the wait times going up.

Second, fix the five things people come for. Burgers, fajitas, Chicken Crispers, margaritas and the Triple Dipper are the “5 to Drive,” and sales in those five categories doubled from $1.2B to $2.4B in three years. The Triple Dipper alone went from $224M to $864M and is now 16% of sales. Only 60% of the menu has been upgraded, which is why the deck talks about years of innovation runway rather than a finished job.

Third, win on value and say so on television. “3 for Me” at $10.99 is 21% of sales. The advertising compares the Big Smasher to a fast-food burger and the Big Crispy to a fast-food chicken sandwich, and the comparison works because the Chili’s version is bigger and arrives at a table.

Top-of-mind awareness went from 37% to 42% and Chili’s now has the number-one share of alcohol servings in casual dining. The per-person average is still below the competition even after the third-party data provider corrected its benchmarks in October.

Fourth, let the margin fund the next round. Higher volumes over a fixed cost base took restaurant margin from 11.2% to 17.8%, FCF from $71M to $558M, and net debt from $907M to $335M.

The flywheel the CEO describes is traffic, then sales, then margin, then reinvestment. That is a description of what happened.

The result is a three-year cumulative comp of 71%, the one chart I’d show anyone who thinks this was a social-media fluke.

The flywheel in numbers

The 2023 Investor Day promised 3-5% revenue growth, 5-8% EBITDA growth and 13-17% EPS growth a year. Management delivered 12%, 35% and 56%.

I don’t lead with a scorecard slide as a rule, but a company that beat its own three-year plan by that margin earns the benefit of the doubt on the next one.

Revenue went from $4.4B in FY2024 to $5.4B in FY2025 and $5.8B in FY2026. Chili’s is $5.4B of that and growing; Maggiano’s is $455M and shrinking. Franchise revenue, the royalties from 370 international and 99 domestic franchised Chili’s, is small but it rides on $1.1B of franchisee sales that grew 16% last year.

ROIC was 7% in FY2023, one point above the cost of capital. It was 25% in FY2026, 17 points above it. That spread, and whether it lasts, is the whole valuation question, so here is the history before the model’s view of the future.

FCF tells the same story from the cash side. $71M in FY2023, $223M, $414M, then $558M in FY2026 on $789M of operating cash flow and $232M of capex. The company spent $444M on buybacks last year and $125M more in Q1, redeemed its $350M 8.25% bonds in July with the revolver, and still has $700M of liquidity.

And the estimates have spent two years chasing the print. Revenue has beaten consensus in 8 of the last 12 quarters…

… and EPS in 10 of 12, the last one by 13%.

The next chapter: three levers Mr. Market isn’t pricing

Everything above is the past. The published debate treats the comp line as the only engine, and asks how long a brand can keep lapping a 21% comp. What matters from here is what the restaurants can produce, and the answer comes in three pieces that the Investor Day laid out and the bear case hasn’t engaged with.

Lever one: throughput. The average Chili’s serves 4,200 guests a week. Its own historical peak was 5,200. Fifteen percent of the system already runs above that peak, which is proof the box can hold it. The gap between 4,200 and 5,200 is 1,000 guests a week, 24% more traffic, with no new building, no new lease and no new manager. The operating initiatives the COO described, host-stand staffing, kitchen display systems, a to-go redesign and a two-to-three-year AI-driven back-of-house system, exist to close that gap. Management put nothing from these in the FY2027 guidance.

Lever two: mix shift into the high-volume cohort. Restaurants above $6M of annual sales run restaurant margins 400bps above the system average, because the fixed costs are the same and the sales are 20% higher. Only 20% of the estate is above $6M today, and the deck says more restaurants cross the line every month. If the average unit goes from $5.0M to $6.0M over the next three years, the margin doesn’t need a new idea; it needs the existing ones to keep working. That is why my base case has restaurant margin reaching 21.5% by FY2031, and why the model flags that number as above anything the company has ever posted. It is. So is $6M of AUV.

Lever three: new units and reimages. Chili’s opened six company restaurants in FY2026 and plans four in FY2027. From FY2028 the pace changes. The target is 30 openings a year by FY2029, 2-3% unit growth, with 300 trade areas already identified for ten years of development, at the unit economics from the P&L section.

On top of that, the reimage program remodels 60-80 restaurants in FY2027 for $42M and ramps to 10% of the fleet a year, 110 units for $66M in FY2028, with a 3-5% sales lift on a $500-600K spend. The CFO said the first 20 reimages are covering their cost of capital and that it is early. I’m treating the reimages as maintenance that happens to lift sales and the new units as the real growth capital.

Put the three together and you get the three-year algorithm management published: 4-6% revenue growth a year, double-digit EPS growth, 3-5% of the shares repurchased annually, and leverage below 2.0x. The EPS number works even on a mid-single-digit comp, because 2% from units plus 4% from comps plus 100bps of margin plus a 4% smaller share count compounds to low teens. My base case is a notch above the algorithm on revenue in FY2027 and in line with it thereafter.

Management and capital allocation

The CEO’s KFC fingerprints are visible: a short list of hero products, a value price point that is defended in advertising rather than discounted, and an obsession with “making the job easier” for the people in the restaurant. He spent a week in October working hourly shifts in two Chili’s. The CFO gives the margin cadence by quarter, names the inflation she has built in, and raised the FY2027 guide in October after one quarter.

Capital allocation has three stated priorities in order: invest for growth, keep the balance sheet strong, return the excess. The record matches the words.

The buyback authorization was raised to $750M in August and the run rate is $125M a quarter, which at the current price retires 1.3% of the shares a quarter, 5% a year.

Insiders have been sellers: 16 sales and no purchases in 90 days, including by the CEO on October 29, the day after the print. The Form 4s behind them are a to-do before anyone calls them routine, and I take the point up in the bear section.

The smaller brand that drags

Maggiano’s is 52 restaurants of Italian-American family-style dining in upscale malls, $9.5M of sales per unit, a $41 check, and 15% of its business from banquets. It is 8% of revenue and it has been shrinking for a year: comps were -3.9% in FY2026 and -3.4% in Q1 FY2027, with traffic down 9% and 5%. Restaurant margin is 10.1% against Chili’s 18.5%, because the same deleverage math that lifts Chili’s runs in reverse at a brand losing guests.

Management calls the turnaround “mixed” and “slower than planned,” which is the right description. The plan is the Chili’s plan a year behind: fix the core menu, speed up service, upgrade the atmosphere, grow the banquet business. The FY2027 guidance assumes flat revenue and profit for the brand. For the model I give Maggiano’s nothing: the consolidated revenue line in the base case is a Chili’s forecast with an 8% passenger that doesn’t grow. If Maggiano’s recovers, it is upside. If it gets sold, it is also upside, because the proceeds would retire shares at a multiple below what the Chili’s business deserves.

Valuation

The published model is here.

It is a ten-year FCFF DCF with three explicit cases, a competitive-fade stage after year ten and a terminal stage where new capital earns only the cost of capital. The base year is FY2026 and the price it is struck on is the $207 close of November 3, 20% below the August high.

The shares rose 5% on November 4, which takes the base-case upside from 19% to 13% at $219; the rating and the fair value don’t change.

Revenue. The base case takes FY2027 at +9.5%, above the top of the $6.2-6.3B guidance range. Q1 came in at +9.4%, Q2 is tracking high-mid single digits on the comp, the 53rd week adds 2% and the 12 franchise restaurants acquired in August add on top. The year after laps the extra week, so +5%. FY2029 and FY2030 are +7% each: 2-3% from the 30 units a year, mid-single-digit comps, and the reimage lift on 10% of the fleet. From there growth fades to 4% by year ten. That is management’s plan delivered in full. Before the Investor Day put published targets and capital behind it, that would have been a bull case; now it is the plan.

The bear case is the plan at its midpoint with no beats: FY2027 at the guidance midpoint of +8%, FY2028 at +3%, then 5%, the low-middle of the 4-6% algorithm, fading to 3%. The bull case is units at 3%+ a year and comps that hold mid-single digits for the decade, +10% in FY2027 and +8% in FY2029-2030.

Margins. The gross margin line in this model is revenue less food, labour and restaurant expenses, so it reads like restaurant operating margin: 18.6% in FY2026. The base case adds the 70-90bps management guided for FY2027, then 40bps a year, the top of the CFO’s “20-40bps on mid-single-digit comps” rule, to 21.5% by FY2031. That is the AUV mix shift from lever two. SG&A holds at 3.9% against a 4.0-4.1% guide and depreciation rises with the capex. EBIT margin goes from 10.7% in FY2026 to 12.0% in FY2027 and 13.3% by FY2031, below the 13.6% the Street already models for FY2030. The bear holds margin at 19.5% to 20.6% and EBIT at 11.7%, the bull reaches 22.5% and 14.5%.

Reinvestment. Capex is 4.4% of revenue in FY2027 on the $265-285M guide, then climbs to 5.6% by FY2030 as the reimages reach 110 a year and the new units reach 30, and eases back to 4.8% once the opening rate flattens. Working capital stays negative, as it always is in a business that collects at the table and pays its suppliers in 13 days.

Discount rate. A 4.9% ten-year Treasury, Damodaran’s 4.2% equity risk premium and a 0.78 unlevered beta for restaurants, relevered to 0.89 on a 16% debt-to-capital weight, give an 8.7% cost of equity. I set the pre-tax cost of debt at 5.5%, the revolver rate now that the 8.25% bonds are gone, rather than the 2.3% the trailing interest line implies. WACC is 8.0%. The equity bridge deducts $1.65B of net debt, which treats the lease liabilities as debt; that is the conservative end of the two ways to do it.

The fade. After year ten the return on new capital walks down to the cost of capital over five years in the base case, which is the reference range for a narrow moat. Three years in the bear, eight in the bull. The moat is narrow because casual dining has no switching costs and the value-plus-marketing model can be copied; it exists at all because the execution behind it takes years to copy, as the turnover and throughput numbers show.

The output. Base case $247 a share, +19% against the $207 close. Bear $188, -9%. Bull $298, +44%. Risk-reward 2.1 to 1, above the 2.0x hurdle RankedStocks sets for a narrow-moat business.

Stage three, the years after the fade, is 41% of enterprise value. That is lower than most DCFs on growth names, because the explicit ten years carry 43% and the fade another 16%. The implied exit multiple is 10.2x EBIT, below where the stock trades today on trailing numbers.

What the price assumes. Run the model backwards and $207 is consistent with 4.2% revenue growth a year for ten years on the base-case margins. The Street models 5.6%. My bear is 4.3%, my base 6.0%. The current price is pricing my bear case on revenue. On the Street comparison, the base case sits above the top of the published analyst range on revenue in all four forecast years and above the consensus mean on EBIT in the first two, which the model flags as “a call no analyst has published.” It is. It is also the company’s own plan.

What moves it. The fair value is most sensitive to the discount rate: 50bps on the WACC is worth $20 a share either way, and even at 9.0% with no fade the value is $204, 2% below the price. Every cell of the sensitivity grid at 8.5% WACC or below beats the current price.

Why the DCF and the consensus disagree in opposite directions. The automatic three-stage DCF on RankedStocks, which plugs in consensus and lets margins revert to the company’s own ten-year history, lands at $155. The sell-side median target is $270. The gap between those two numbers is the gap between a model that assumes the last decade’s margins come back and a model that assumes the last three years’ margins stay. My $247 is a view that the rebuilt margin is structural, because turnover, throughput and AUV are structural.

Steel-manning the bear

Six arguments, each at full strength, each with my answer.

The comps are about to lap themselves. Chili’s comped +21% in Q1 FY2026 and +10% on top of that. From Q2 the comparison gets harder every quarter, management itself guides mid-single digits for the rest of the year, and November 2025 was a huge month to lap. A brand running +6% traffic can’t do it forever, and when the comp prints +3%, the multiple that was built on +10% comes down with it.

My answer: the base case already assumes it. FY2028 revenue growth is +5% with the 53rd week lapped, and the three years after that lean on units and reimages rather than on comps above mid-single digits. The comp deceleration is the consensus view and it is in the price; a 4.2% implied revenue growth rate is a market that expects the comps to fade to low single digits and the unit program not to show up.

The valuation is rich for a restaurant. At 19.7x forward earnings EAT trades at a premium to its own five-year average of 17.4x and to most of casual dining, and the EV/sales multiple of 1.8x is above its history. The stock is up 97% in a year. Mean reversion in restaurant multiples is a fact of life.

My answer: the five-year average multiple was earned on 11% restaurant margins and a $3.3M AUV. The business that earns 18% margins on $5.0M AUV and retires 4% of its shares a year is a different business and deserves a different multiple. The comparison I’d make is against the cash: at $207 the equity is 16x FY2026 FCF and the FCF yield is 6%, for a company growing FCF at double digits with leverage at 0.4x. The forward P/E is the Street’s way of saying “restaurant.”

Chili’s carries the whole company. There is no second engine. Maggiano’s is shrinking and the international franchise business is small. If Chili’s stumbles, nothing offsets it.

My answer: true, and it cuts both ways. Concentration in the best-run brand in the category is a feature in a consolidation; concentration in a brand that loses relevance is the whole bear case. I size the position for that, and the bear case in the model is a Chili’s that hits its plan rather than one that beats it.

Insiders are selling into the buyback. Sixteen sales and zero buys in 90 days, including the CEO the day after the Q1 print. The company spent $444M buying what its executives were selling.

My answer: grants made when the stock was a fifth of today’s price are vesting into a stock up 97% in a year, and selling some is what a rational executive does. The CEO’s pay package is two-thirds equity, so his incentives still point the right way. But I don’t dismiss it. An insider buy at these prices would strengthen the case and there hasn’t been one. The buyback decision is made by a board that just raised the authorization to $750M with the stock at $200, which is its own signal.

The consumer is cracking, and beef is at a record. Management already sees check management in alcohol and dessert. Gas is $4.29. Sentiment is the second-lowest on record. Cattle supply won’t recover for two years, and 3-4% commodity inflation on a brand that refuses to pass it through ends in margin compression. The “value leader” positioning is a promise to eat the inflation.

My answer: this is the strongest bear argument, and the model’s bear case is where I put it: margin flat at 19.5-20.6% for a decade, no leverage from AUV growth, and it still produces $188 a share, 9% below the price. Chili’s absorbed 4.4% commodity inflation in Q4 FY2026 and 3.3% in Q1 and expanded margin both times, because traffic grew faster than cost. The risk is a quarter where traffic turns negative, and that is the signal I watch above every other.

The capex ramp will dilute returns. Capex goes from $232M to $400M+ as reimages hit 110 a year and units hit 30. The CFO couldn’t give remodel returns beyond “covering the cost of capital.” Restaurant chains have a long history of growing into mediocre returns.

My answer: the model charges all of it. Capex rises to 5.6% of revenue, FCF conversion drops with it, and the fair value is still $247. The new units carry a published 18-20% cash-on-cash hurdle against an 8% cost of capital and 300 trade areas to choose from. If the 3-5% lift doesn’t hold the capex still had to be spent to keep the boxes relevant.

The Monte Carlo: 10,000 runs

The simulation re-runs the base case 10,000 times with the five inputs that matter drawn from distributions bracketed by the bear and bull cases: ten-year average revenue growth between 4.3% and 7.0%, average EBIT margin between 11.9% and 13.9%, WACC normal around 8.0% with a 0.5-point standard deviation, the fade between zero and ten years, and capex between 5.0% and 5.4% of revenue. I correlated revenue growth with EBIT margin at 0.5, because in this business more guests means more margin, and with capex at 0.5, because more growth means more building. Latin hypercube sampling, antithetic variates, seed 2026 so you can reproduce it on RankedStocks.

The distribution clears today’s price in 89% of runs. The 5th percentile is $198, 5% below the price; the 95th is $289. The median sits $8 below the deterministic base, which says the base case is a touch generous rather than a touch mean. The three marked lines show the bear case landing inside the first decile and the bull case at the 97th percentile, so the deterministic cases bracket the simulation rather than sitting at its extremes.

Sixty-one percent of the spread comes from the discount rate rather than from the operating assumptions. That is what it means to own a business whose cash flows are predictable: the argument is about what the money is worth rather than whether the restaurants earn it. Revenue growth is a fifth of the spread and margin an eighth. Whatever discount rate you use, the thesis rests on a Chili's at $5M of sales and 18% margins staying a Chili's.

From HOLD to BUY

I set a $225 target when I picked EAT in 2024 and the shares went through it. From there the stock was a HOLD: the business kept beating, the price kept catching up, and the model I had valued the comp line and little else. A HOLD on a stock that is up 330% is a decision to keep the position and stop adding, and that was right while the price ran ahead of the plan I could underwrite.

Three things changed between August and today. The Investor Day on September 17 turned the bull case into the plan: unit growth, reimages and the buyback went from my hopes for the next chapter to published targets with capital behind them, from a team that beat its last three-year plan by a wide margin. The price then fell 20% from the August high while the quarter that followed beat and the guide went up. And I rebuilt the model on FCF with the reinvestment in it, which is where the $247, the $188 bear and the 2.1 to 1 ratio in the Valuation section come from.

Verdict

I’m moving EAT from HOLD to BUY with a fair value of $247.

Sterling Infrastructure [] and Dell [] sit in the portfolio with a path to a double, and here I am upgrading a name with 19% upside. The two returns carry different risk. STRL and DELL, like POWL and CLS, sell into the datacenter build-out, and their doubles depend on that capex cycle holding for another two or three years. EAT’s cash flows depend on a Tuesday night at a Chili’s. With a bear case 9% below the price, an 89% Monte Carlo hit rate, 0.4x leverage and a 6% FCF yield, 19% is worth as much to me on a risk-adjusted basis as a double that rides a cycle, and it is a return that doesn’t move with the rest of the book: a Chili’s fills up when a family that was headed to a drive-through sits down for $10.99 instead.

The 19% is also the floor of what I think is there. The model gives Maggiano’s zero, puts nothing in for the 1,000 guests a week of throughput headroom in the existing boxes, counts no value from buying back 4% of the shares a year below fair value, and treats $1.2B of operating leases as debt in the equity bridge, which on its own is $27 a share. None of that is in the $247. That is my margin of safety, and it is why the rating is BUY rather than a HOLD with a higher target.

If this changed how you look at the next restaurant print, send it to one person who owns a casual-dining name.
